newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Frost sees victories in UK petrol war.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Frost sees victories in UK petrol war.

text.p: A price war in the British petrol market could reward surviving oil companies with greater profits in 1997, the largest independent retailer, Frost Group Plc, said on Friday.
But the number of British petrol stations is likely to fall this year at a similar rate to 1996, when nearly 10 percent, or 1,500 sites closed, said chairman James Frost.

"Those sites that survive will sell more petrol at higher prices and margins, and therefore be more valuable," Frost said. "The facts are that there are fewer sites, fewer suppliers and real growth in the size of the overall market for the first time in seven years."

He predicted higher profits, earnings and dividends for Frost Group in 1997 after earlier announcing that pretax profits slipped last year to 10.4 million pounds ($16.6 million) from 11.1 million the previous year.
Frost said his company had refused to cut its prices despite lower sales.
Esso Petroleum's Pricewatch campaign, launched in early 1996 with a promise to match its lowest-priced competitors, helped to squeeze fuel margins to break-even levels last summer.
Many independent retailers closed because they could not compete with the big oil companies and the low-cost supermarkets.

A recovery in margins at the end of last year was likely continue, Frost said, helped by a strong British economy. Another boost may come if crude oil prices, which jumped to six-year highs in 1996, continued to pull back while pump prices stabilised, thereby helping margins, he said.
The company, which proposed changing its name to Save Group Plc to match its petrol brand, has shut 30 company-owned sites and cut its dealer network to around 200 sites.
The total number of stations displaying the Save/Burmah brand is about 614, ranking it eighth among British retailers. Esso, a unit of U.S. oil giant Exxon Corp, is still number one with 1,980 sites.
